extracted.intended_audience: novelists, creative-writing students, and serious readers/critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for writing and evaluating novels, focusing on character types (flat vs round), point of view, interiority, and the nature and construction of plot. Emphasizes practical devices novelists use to harmonize characters with plot and to engage readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters should parallel, not coincide, with daily life
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not expect novel-characters to coincide as a whole with daily life; they should parallel it and adapt to requirements of the creator (plot, moral, atmosphere, fellow characters).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Characters must be shaped to serve other aspects of the novel: they may be realistic in bits but as wholes will be tailored to the book's needs. This implies interdependence (e.g., Austen's characters) rather than isolable, transplantable figures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of flat characters (types / humours)
rubrics_metrics.description: Flat characters are constructed round a single idea or quality and can be expressed in one sentence (e.g., 'I never will desert Mr. Micawber').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Advantages: instantly recognizable, need no reintroduction, provide atmosphere, easily remembered, and useful for economy and permanence. Best used for comic effects or where stability is desired. Disadvantages: not great for serious or tragic long performance — they bore if used too seriously. Useful in combination with round characters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of round characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Round characters are complex, cannot be summed up in a single phrase, and are capable of surprising the reader in a convincing way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Roundness is tested by the character's capacity to surprise convincingly; they are suited to depth and tragedy and can expand under novelistic circumstances. If a character never surprises it is flat; if it surprises but does not convince it is a failed attempt at roundness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix flat and round characters appropriately
rubrics_metrics.description: A novel often requires both flat and round people; collisions between different kinds of characters help the novel 'acclimatize' and can parallel life more accurately.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Flat characters supply immediate recognition and stability while round characters supply depth; using both in combination (as Dickens or Austen do) can achieve various effects, from vivid vitality to organized subtlety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characters must be integrated/inter-dependent within the novel
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be tied into the fabric of the novel (linked to plot and other characters) rather than free-floating; some characters cannot be 'transplanted' without bringing an ensemble with them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interdependence preserves internal probability and texture (e.g., Miss Bates is linked to Highbury). In ensemble novels characters must exercise mutual restraint and function as parts of a closely woven fabric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance authorial control vs characters' autonomy
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters are creations inside a creation; if given complete freedom they may 'run away' and ruin the book, but if kept too sternly in check they may 'die' or cause decay.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novelist must manage the tension between letting characters act naturally and ensuring they contribute to the larger scheme—too much freedom or too much restraint both harm the work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Point of view: choose and manage narrator's relation to the story
rubrics_metrics.description: Points of view include outside description (impartial/partial observer), omniscience, inhabiting a character (dramatic/first-person), and intermediate attitudes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shifting viewpoints are acceptable if the author has the power to 'bounce' the reader into accepting them; the choice shapes method and must serve the novel's emotional and aesthetic aims rather than call attention to itself.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid taking the reader into confidence about individual characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Authorial confidences about individuals (asides that reveal the novelist's private judgments or favourites) are dangerous and tend to cool the creative illusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such confidences often lead to facetiousness and intellectual laxity. Generalized confidences about the universe or condition are less harmful and can be acceptable (e.g., Hardy, Conrad). Keep intimate asides to a minimum to preserve illusion and nobility.

rubrics_metrics.name: The novelist must be able to 'bounce' the reader when shifting viewpoint
rubrics_metrics.description: The central power in method is the writer's ability to make the reader accept shifts of stance or knowledge—i.e., to 'bounce' the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the writer can convincingly move between omniscience, partial omniscience, and dramatic presentation (as Dickens or Tolstoy do), then logical incoherence in method becomes tolerable; but if the reader is caught and not bounced, the effect fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of interiority and secret life (access to soliloquy and subconscious)
rubrics_metrics.description: The novel's speciality is access to characters' secret, interior life—self-communings and subconscious—material unavailable to drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The novelist should exploit interiority to enrich character and motive; shifts between limited and omniscient presentation of interior states are permissible provided they are convincing and not obviously inconsistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish story (time-sequence) from plot (causality)
rubrics_metrics.description: A story is a sequence of events ('and then...'); a plot emphasizes causality and asks 'why?'—it suspends simple chronology to reveal causes and relations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding this distinction guides how to organize material: plots manipulate time and create mystery and causal chains, whereas stories merely record succession.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot must demand intelligence and memory from the reader
rubrics_metrics.description: A true plot requires reader intelligence to hold and relate clues and memory to recall earlier facts so causality can be perceived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers must be expected to remember prior details; a plot that relies on intelligence and memory can use cross-correspondences and delayed revelations (mystery pockets) to create aesthetic payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy, organic unity, and no loose ends in plot construction
rubrics_metrics.description: Every action or word in the plot ought to count; the plot should be economical, spare, organic, and free from 'dead matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even in complexity the novel should avoid misleading the reader and should rearrange clues into an aesthetically compact whole—beauty in plot is an emergent effect of careful construction, not its ostensible goal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mystery (suspension of chronology) as a plot device
rubrics_metrics.description: Mystery is a 'pocket in time'—suspending sequence to create questions (e.g., 'Why did the queen die?') that demand intelligence and memory to resolve.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Well-used mystery can provide depth and aesthetic surprise; to be effective it must be planted and later illuminated so the reader's recollection and intelligence can assemble causality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aim for convincing shifts between limited and omniscient presentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Shifts into characters' minds and back out (limited to omniscient) are acceptable provided they are convincing and do not sound like legalistic questioning of standpoint.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The reader cares whether the shifting of attitude and the handling of secret life are convincing; technique should be subordinated to emotional truth rather than rigid formal consistency.
